findings.title: Idle DynamoDB Table
findings.action: Delete or switch to on-demand billing.

explanation.detection: Zero consumed read and write capacity over 14 days (10 RCU / 10 WCU provisioned), on a table 96 days old
explanation.threshold: 0 consumed reads AND 0 consumed writes over a 14-day monitoring period, on a table at least 14 days old
explanation.pricing: Provisioned: $5.69/month for idle capacity
explanation.why_waste: This table has had no reads or writes in 14 days. Provisioned capacity charges continue regardless of usage.
explanation.risk: Verify no applications depend on this table. Check DynamoDB Streams consumers. If keeping, switch to on-demand to avoid idle costs.

findings.title: DynamoDB Table Without Auto-Scaling
findings.action: Enable auto-scaling or switch to on-demand billing.
findings.actionCommand: aws application-autoscaling register-scalable-target --service-namespace dynamodb --resource-id table/<DynamoDB table B> --scalable-dimension dynamodb:table:ReadCapacityUnits --min-capacity 1 --max-capacity 10

explanation.detection: Provisioned mode with 10 RCU / 10 WCU and no Application Auto Scaling target registered
explanation.threshold: Provisioned table with monthly cost ≥ $5 and no auto-scaling
explanation.pricing: Provisioned: (10 RCU × $0.00013 + 10 WCU × $0.00065) × 730 = $5.69/month. ~15% savings with auto-scaling: $0.85/month
explanation.why_waste: Without auto-scaling, provisioned capacity is fixed 24/7. Auto-scaling adjusts capacity based on traffic, reducing cost during low-activity periods.
explanation.risk: Auto-scaling has a brief delay when scaling up. Set appropriate minimum capacities for baseline traffic. Consider on-demand mode as an alternative.

findings.title: S3 Rapid Growth Anomaly
findings.action: S3 bucket 'S3 bucket D' grew from under 0.1 GB to 12.0 GB in 30 days (+12.0 GB). Investigate source of growth. Consider adding lifecycle rules to expire old objects or transition to cheaper storage classes.

explanation.detection: Bucket grew from under 0.1 GB to 12.0 GB in 30 days (+12.0 GB)
explanation.threshold: > 100.0% growth in 30 days with > 10.0 GB absolute increase
explanation.pricing: Growth adds ~$0.28/month in storage costs.
explanation.why_waste: Abnormal growth often indicates runaway logging, build artifacts, or misconfigured data pipelines. Without lifecycle rules, this growth continues unchecked.
explanation.risk: Investigate the source of growth before adding lifecycle rules. Use S3 Storage Lens or S3 Inventory to identify which prefixes are growing.

findings.title: Unattached EBS Volume (1GB gp3)
findings.action: Delete this volume if no longer needed.

explanation.detection: EBS volume state is "available" (not attached to any EC2 instance)
explanation.threshold: Volume not attached to any instance
explanation.why_waste: This volume is not attached to any instance. It was likely left behind after an instance was terminated or a snapshot was restored.
explanation.risk: Verify no data on this volume is needed before deleting. Consider creating a snapshot first as a safety net.

findings.title: Old/Untagged ECR Images
findings.action: Delete old images or set up lifecycle policy.

explanation.detection: 1 untagged and 0 old images totaling 0.6 GB
explanation.threshold: > 0.5 GB of old/untagged images
explanation.pricing: 0.6 GB × $0.10/GB/month = $0.06/month
explanation.why_waste: Untagged images are typically superseded builds. Old images beyond your rollback window serve no purpose.
explanation.risk: Verify no running tasks reference these images. Keep the latest tagged images needed for production and rollback.

findings.title: Orphaned EBS Snapshot (1GB)

findings.title: Untagged ECR Images
findings.action: Delete untagged images or add a lifecycle policy to expire them automatically.
findings.actionCommand: aws ecr batch-delete-image --repository-name <ECR repository C> --image-ids "$(aws ecr list-images --repository-name <ECR repository C> --filter tagStatus=UNTAGGED --query 'imageIds[*]' --output json)"

explanation.detection: 1 images without any tag in repository 'ECR repository C' (0.21 GB)
explanation.threshold: > 0 untagged images with > 0.1 GB total size
explanation.pricing: 0.21 GB × $0.10/GB/month = $0.02/month
explanation.why_waste: Untagged images are created when a new image is pushed with the same tag, replacing the old manifest. The old image loses its tag but remains stored. These orphaned layers accumulate and increase storage costs.
explanation.risk: Untagged images cannot be pulled by tag. They are only referenced by digest. Verify no Fargate tasks or Kubernetes pods reference images by SHA digest before deleting.

findings.title: EFS Without Mount Targets
findings.action: Delete this filesystem.
findings.actionCommand: aws efs delete-file-system --file-system-id <EFS file system A>

explanation.detection: EFS filesystem has no mount targets (not mounted anywhere)
explanation.threshold: Zero mount targets with size > $0 cost
explanation.pricing: 0.0 GB × $0.30/GB/month = $0.01/month
explanation.why_waste: Without mount targets, no EC2 instance or container can access this filesystem. It's paying for storage that cannot be read or written.
explanation.risk: Verify the filesystem is not in the process of being set up. Back up data with AWS Backup or DataSync before deleting.

findings.title: Excessive Lambda Timeout
findings.action: Reduce timeout from 900s to 10s (3× the longest observed invocation).

explanation.detection: Timeout is 900s but average execution is 3ms (293160× ratio)
explanation.threshold: Timeout ≥ 10× average duration and ≥ 60s, and 3× the longest observed invocation is below the current timeout
explanation.pricing: Risk exposure: $0.01/month if 1% of invocations hang to full timeout
explanation.why_waste: An excessive timeout means a stuck invocation burns Lambda compute for 900s instead of failing fast. This is a cost-risk and operational-reliability finding.
explanation.risk: The longest invocation in the last 30 days took 20ms; the recommended 10s is at least 3× that. Rarer, longer invocations outside this window would fail at the new timeout.

explanation.pricing: Risk exposure: $0.01/month if 1% of invocations hang to full timeout

explanation.risk: The longest invocation in the last 30 days took 120234ms; the recommended 361s is at least 3× that. Rarer, longer invocations outside this window would fail at the new timeout.

findings.title: Deprecated Lambda Runtime
findings.action: Update the runtime. EOL 2025-12-15. Migrate to python3.13.

explanation.detection: Function uses deprecated runtime python3.9
explanation.threshold: Runtime is past AWS end-of-life date
explanation.pricing: $0.01/month (hygiene finding: no direct cost savings)
explanation.why_waste: Deprecated runtimes no longer receive security patches from AWS. EOL 2025-12-15. Migrate to python3.13.
explanation.risk: Runtime migration may require code changes. Test thoroughly in a staging environment. Check for deprecated API usage in your function code.

findings.title: Incomplete Multipart Uploads
findings.action: Abort the stale multipart uploads, and add a lifecycle rule (AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload after 7 days) so new ones are cleaned up.

explanation.detection: 1 of the bucket's 1 incomplete multipart uploads were started more than 7 days ago
explanation.threshold: Incomplete multipart uploads older than 7 days
explanation.pricing: Uploaded parts are billed as S3 storage until the upload is aborted, but their size is not measured: reading it needs s3:ListMultipartUploadParts, which the CloudWise scan role does not have. Saving shown as $0; the S3 Storage Lens "incomplete multipart upload bytes" metric shows the real figure.
explanation.why_waste: Incomplete multipart uploads consume storage but are not usable. They are typically left behind by failed or interrupted uploads.
explanation.risk: Aborting a stale upload is safe; uploads under 7 days old are not flagged, since they may still be in progress. A lifecycle rule prevents future accumulation.
